tldr: Gamov (LangChain4j) and Sadogursky (Koog) build the same personal 'claw' agent side by side in seven stages, from chatbot to multi-model workflow with human review and Langfuse tracing.
summary: Viktor Gamov and Baruch Sadogursky build "J.Claw", a joke personal assistant that writes excuses to get them out of a mandatory AI-proficiency training run by "Dana from People Ops". Gamov codes it in Java with LangChain4j, Sadogursky in Kotlin with JetBrains Koog. Both use the same Gemini Flash model, the same prompt and a terminal UI built with Cédric Champeau's TamboUI. After each stage the audience votes. The first stage is the two-line chatbot: an annotated AI service in LangChain4j, an explicit agent builder in Koog. Because it has no context, the bot invents a plausible excuse but has no idea who Dana is.

Next come tools: calendar and contacts/email stubs packaged as MCP servers. Sadogursky runs them as separate JVM processes that talk over stdio, while Gamov shows that plain annotated Java methods can also be tools. The model only expresses an intent to call a tool, and the application runs it. Memory follows. LangChain4j uses a MessageWindowChatMemory of 30 messages plus a local tool over a JSON-lines file of past excuses. Koog uses a flat-file conversation store and an embedding-based vector store for long-term memory. With memory in place, the agent finally avoids reusing excuses. Agent skills come next: a "corporate speak" skill, loaded through progressive discovery of its front-matter description, rewrites any text on a jargon scale from 1 to 11.

After the break the talk moves to agentic workflows. A cheap, fast classification model routes the request (about 16 ms, with confidence scores) to either chat or a decline flow. In the decline flow Claude drafts the email and Codex reviews it in a bounded refine loop. Koog builds this as a strongly typed graph of nodes and edges, checked at compile time. LangChain4j uses its agentic module's sequence, loop, parallel and conditional workflows, plus a new decision-model primitive. A human-in-the-loop node adds a second approval before sending. Observability comes from Koog's OpenTelemetry feature exporting to Langfuse, where the trace shows the whole run at about 3,000 tokens. LangChain4j uses an agent listener, an HTML report generator and Micrometer.

No framework wins the final vote, and the speakers conclude that JVM developers now have several mature agent frameworks. Sadogursky then rebuilds the same workflow without code in Port, his employer's platform, generated by an agent over Port's MCP server. In the Q&A both argue that context matters more than raw model strength: a weak model given skills and tools comes close to a frontier model without them. They see company model bans as mostly about cost, and suggest debugging agent apps with existing JVM tooling (debugger, JFR) exposed to agents through MCP.
keyPoints: Both frameworks need only a few lines per capability: a chat model, then memory, then tools, then skills, plugged into the same agent builder. LangChain4j uses annotations such as @SystemMessage; Koog uses explicit Kotlin builders and installable features.
MCP servers can be plain JARs launched as child processes and spoken to over stdin/stdout. The LLM API never calls the tool itself; the agent application does.

LLM calls are stateless, so conversation memory has to be resent with every call. That is why context windows fill up, and why the speakers present summarisation of old conversations into long-term memory as an unsolved problem.

Skills are Markdown files with a YAML front-matter description; only the descriptions load at start-up and the body loads when a request matches. Sadogursky's eval showed his Koog-authoring skill lifting success to 92% (about 7x), because Koog is too new to be in model training data.

Routing with a classification-only model is fast and cheap. Koog had no built-in support for the new model, so Sadogursky wrapped its public protocol himself. LangChain4j had just added a 'decision model' type for such models.

Koog's crown jewel is its typed strategy graph; LangChain4j's agentic module offers sequential, loop, parallel, conditional and goal-oriented workflows, and Embabel takes a single goal-oriented approach.
Sadogursky showed roughly $20,000 of monthly usage that would have been billed at API rates but was covered by flat Claude and Codex subscriptions, which both frameworks can use.
Live demos hit provider outages and overly strict reviewer loops (six rejected refinements), showing why bounded loops and tracing matter.
takeaways: Keep deterministic business steps as plain code and use LLMs only at the fuzzy edges (drafting, summarising, interpreting tool output).
Route requests with a cheap classifier or small model before calling expensive frontier models.
Write agent skills for any library newer than your model's training data, and measure them with an eval with and without the skill.
Cap reviewer/refine loops and add a human approval step before any agent action with side effects such as sending email.
Instrument agent workflows with OpenTelemetry (for example to Langfuse) so you can see routing decisions, prompts and token cost per run.

quotes.text: The speed of coding was never a problem. Let's face it.
Context is what makes or breaks your usage of a model.
Harness and context are much more important than the smartness of the model itself.

watchIf: You want to add agent features to a JVM app and are choosing between LangChain4j and Koog, or want to see tools, memory, skills, routing and tracing built up step by step.
